entries.clue: Greek god of love to go on a survey (6)

indicatorNotes.to go on: What goes on a thing is written after it in an across answer, so the letter named is sent to the back.

blocks.note: a poll is a survey of opinion, its two words run together
love is nothing on a tennis scoreboard, and nothing is written as a nought

annotation.surface: A god of love sent out to conduct a piece of market research.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Greek god of love' reads as one phrase and the love belongs to the wordplay instead — the god of that is Eros. O for love comes from tennis, where a nil score is called love.
annotation.definitionFit: Apollo is one of the twelve Olympians, god of the sun, music and prophecy, so Greek god names him by his class.

indicatorNotes.about: About means moving from place to place, and letters sent about do not come back in the order they left in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: Somebody telling lies about an old variety of pear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fibbing about' is ordinary English and the eye runs straight over it, which is exactly where the instruction is hiding. The fodder is the full thirteen letters, so nothing else has to be found once it is spotted.
annotation.definitionFit: Prevarication is the act of dodging the truth with evasive half-answers, and fibbing is the everyday word for the same behaviour.

indicatorNotes.about: Someone who moves about does not stay where they were put, and neither do letters told to do it.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: A boy caught telling untruths about a big cat.
annotation.walkthrough: Son is S in nearly every grid, so the hard part is taking the whole word as fodder rather than one letter of it. Seven letters is the length where an anagram stops being visible on the page.
annotation.definitionFit: Lion, tiger and leopard are the big cats, and this is the female lion, so the definition names her by her group.

indicatorNotes.outing: An outing takes a thing out of its usual place, and letters taken out of place come back in a new order.

blocks.note: to opt for something is to choose it
the four letters of LIMA rearranged

annotation.surface: Picking the day trip to the Peruvian capital as the one to go on.
annotation.walkthrough: Lima is the radio alphabet's L before it is anywhere in Peru, and that single letter is the trap — all four are wanted here. Outing is doing the shuffling while looking like part of the holiday.
annotation.definitionFit: Optimal means the best available in the circumstances, the word an engineer reaches for where everyone else says best.

entries.clue: Form you begin to find stylish (6)

indicatorNotes.begin: Where a word begins is the single letter it starts with, so only that letter is taken from the word in front.

blocks.note: a form at a British school is a class of pupils — the fourth form
the letter YOU starts with

annotation.surface: A shape you gradually come round to admiring.
annotation.walkthrough: You is U in most grids and here it is wanted for its first letter instead, which is the whole difficulty in four words. Form for class is school vocabulary, not paperwork.
annotation.definitionFit: Classy describes a thing with style and quality about it, so stylish drops straight into its place as an adjective.

entries.clue: Insensitive fool given little credit at first (5)

indicatorNotes.at first: At first here says where a piece stands rather than what is taken from it, sending the credit to the front.

blocks.note: cr is the bookkeeper's short form of credit, and little asks for the short form
an ass is a fool, the donkey borrowed for a stupid person

annotation.surface: A dolt being handed hardly any credit for what he did.
annotation.walkthrough: At first looks like the standard instruction to take an initial letter, and it is marking a position instead. Cr is the credit column of a ledger, the dr and cr of double-entry bookkeeping.
annotation.definitionFit: Crass means coarse and stupidly unfeeling, which is what is meant by calling a remark insensitive.

indicatorNotes.Some: Some of a phrase is a part of it lifted out unbroken, so the letters are already sitting there in order.

blocks.note: five letters running on from inside the first word into the second; the comma counts for nothing

annotation.surface: A butcher running through the cuts: shank, leg, a joint for Sunday.
annotation.walkthrough: Shank, leg and joint are all butcher's words, and joint is the one made to switch back to the body — the hinge rather than the roast. Some is the quiet flag that no letters need moving.
annotation.definitionFit: The ankle is the hinge between leg and foot, so joint names it as a part of the skeleton rather than a cut of meat.

indicatorNotes.breaks: What breaks comes apart into pieces, and the answer is built back up from the pieces rather than from the word whole.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: A bold pair of headphones snapping and reducing their owner to tears.
annotation.walkthrough: Breaks is the sentence's own verb, which is what makes it so easy to read past as the instruction. An enumeration with a lone 1 in the middle nearly always means a phrase built round A.
annotation.definitionFit: To shed a tear is to cry, and sobbing names the same weeping, both standing as the -ing form.

entries.clue: Make one melt with a drink (5,3)

indicatorNotes.Make: Make is an instruction to build something new, and what it builds here is a fresh arrangement of the letters offered.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
the article joins the fodder as its eighth letter

annotation.surface: Charming somebody into melting over a drink together.
annotation.walkthrough: Melt looks exactly like an anagram indicator and is fodder instead, the real instruction being the first word. Make one melt is also the sentence's own idiom for winning a person over.
annotation.definitionFit: Lemon tea is black tea served with a slice of lemon in place of milk, so drink names it by its class.

indicatorNotes.about: About in its other sense means round the outside, so the word in front is opened up and closes over the letter behind.

blocks.note: ken is knowledge — a thing beyond my ken is beyond what I know
the Orient is the East, and east is E on any compass

annotation.surface: Somebody hungry to learn about the Far East.
annotation.walkthrough: About shuffles letters twice elsewhere in this grid and wraps them round something here, and only the fit decides which. Orient is placed to read as the verb, to orient yourself, and is the noun for the East.
annotation.definitionFit: Keen means eager and enthusiastic — a keen student and an eager one are the same pupil.

indicatorNotes.change: A change swaps one arrangement for another, so the letters are handed back in a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters

annotation.surface: Noticing a shift towards taking more time off.
annotation.walkthrough: Change sits where the sentence wants a noun and works as the verb that rearranges. Four-letter anagrams hide well because there is so little to move.
annotation.definitionFit: A life of ease is a life of leisure — both name freedom from work rather than the comfort sense of ease.

indicatorNotes.worried: Worried means pulled about and gnawed at, the way a dog worries a rag, so the letters are left in disarray.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Asking whether the young lady in distress is anxious about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash makes the clue look like two separate remarks, and the second is simply eight letters and the word that muddles them. A damsel is never anything but in distress, which is the phrase the surface leans on.
annotation.definitionFit: To mislead a person is to send them astray, the verb and the phrase swapping places in a sentence about wrong directions.

indicatorNotes.out: To be out is to be wrong or out of true, so the letters in front are not left standing in the order given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: Being told to keep an ear open for the Christmas decorations.
annotation.walkthrough: Listen out for is one idiom in the mouth and the instruction is the single word sitting in its middle. Listen also invites a hunt for a homophone, and there is no sound anywhere in this clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Tinsel is the glittering strip wound round a tree in December, so the definition names it by the job it is bought for.

entries.clue: Motorbike races finish after one – be there (6)

indicatorNotes.after: After tells you which side a piece lands on: what comes after the one is written behind it, leaving the one in front.

blocks.note: one of a thing is a of it — a dozen eggs is one dozen
the TT is the Tourist Trophy, the motorbike races run on the Isle of Man's public roads each summer
the finish of a race is its end

annotation.surface: Motorbike racing that wraps up some time after one o'clock.
annotation.walkthrough: One is the hour on a clock in the surface and a single letter in the wordplay, and after is not joinery but the word that puts that letter first. The Isle of Man TT is Britain's road-racing fortnight.
annotation.definitionFit: To attend a meeting is to be there in person, which is the plain sense wanted rather than attending to something.

entries.clue: Such a case for one at embassy (7)

blocks.note: the slim flat briefcase that carries documents, named after the men who carried them
a junior diplomat on an ambassador's staff, usually with a speciality — military, cultural, press

annotation.surface: A particular sort of case wanted by somebody working at an embassy.
annotation.walkthrough: Such a case leans on the compound attaché case, where the word names the bag only when case follows it. Both halves come from the French for one attached to a mission.
annotation.definitionFit: An attaché is a specialist posted to an embassy's staff, and an attaché case is the slim document briefcase named after them.

entries.clue: Stories about part of Bible and gifts (7)

indicatorNotes.about: What you write about a subject goes round it, so the first word is opened up and closes round what follows.

blocks.note: tales are stories
NT is the New Testament, the Bible's second half

annotation.surface: Stories concerning a section of scripture, and the presents handed out with them.
annotation.walkthrough: Part of Bible is the New Testament shortened the way a chapter heading shortens it. A talent in the Bible is a weight of silver, and the parable of the servants given them is how the word came to mean a gift.
annotation.definitionFit: A talent is a natural aptitude for something — a talent for music is a gift for it, plural answering plural.

indicatorNotes.during: During means in the course of a thing rather than before or after it, so the piece named goes inside the one that follows.

blocks.note: a flight is a journey made by air
an is one of English's three articles, the one used before a vowel

annotation.surface: A window with a newspaper piece propped up in it during a trip.
annotation.walkthrough: Article is almost always A, AN or THE in a grid and hardly ever a piece of journalism, which is what the surface is selling. The name comes from the glazing bars of the old semicircular ones, spread like a fan.
annotation.definitionFit: A fanlight is the window set above a front door to light the hall behind it, so the definition names it by its class.

indicatorNotes.Loudly: Loudly asks for a word said out loud, so what is wanted is spelt differently from the word that makes the sound.

blocks.note: a cat drinks by lapping, so drinks gives LAPS; the word said that way carries a silent letter on the end

annotation.surface: Somebody noisily knocking back drinks, and doing it in error.
annotation.walkthrough: Two spellings, one sound: the extra letter is silent and changes nothing in the mouth. Drinks reads as the noun on the tray and is wanted as the verb an animal does at a bowl.
annotation.definitionFit: A lapse is a slip or small failure of attention — a lapse of memory is a mistake of memory, both nouns.

entries.clue: Hang out round a country in Africa (5)

indicatorNotes.out: Out of order is the sense wanted, so the letters in front of it are not left standing as they were given.
indicatorNotes.round: Round means encircling, so the letters just rearranged are written closing round what comes next.

blocks.note: the four letters of HANG rearranged
the article taken as the single letter it is

annotation.surface: Loafing about somewhere on the African continent.
annotation.walkthrough: Hang out round is exactly how you would describe someone loitering, and all three of those words are working: two instructions and four letters. The article is the only piece taken as it stands.
annotation.definitionFit: Ghana is the West African republic on the Gulf of Guinea, so the definition places it by continent.

indicatorNotes.Audible: Audible asks for what the ear hears rather than what the page shows, so the spelling wanted is not the spelling given.

blocks.note: single means LONE, as in a lone traveller; said aloud it is spelt another way entirely

annotation.surface: A solitary step forward, made loudly enough to be heard.
annotation.walkthrough: Advance looks like the forward move in the surface and the money sense is the one wanted. Single for lone is the step to take before any sound helps.
annotation.definitionFit: An advance is money handed over before it is due, which is what a publisher pays and a bank lends.

entries.clue: One member from West is a weakling (4)

indicatorNotes.from: From says where a piece arrives from, and the west end of an across answer is its left-hand end, so that letter leads.

blocks.note: the compass point in its usual single letter
the Roman numeral for one
a Member of Parliament, the member of a British constituency

annotation.surface: A lone backbencher from a western seat turning out to have no fight in him.
annotation.walkthrough: Member is MP in nearly every British grid, and the surface's solitary politician is built to hide it. The west end of an across entry is its left-hand end, which is where that compass letter goes.
annotation.definitionFit: A wimp is somebody with no backbone or fight in them, which is what calling a person a weakling says.

blocks.note: the clue's own word, taken as it stands
C is the Roman hundred, and a hundred is the grid's shorthand for a lot
what has finished has ended

annotation.surface: Numbers rising just as plenty of other people were finishing.
annotation.walkthrough: Many for C is Roman arithmetic borrowed for the grid, the same trick that makes M a thousand. The clue runs as one unbroken sentence, so the definition has to be cut off after its first two words.
annotation.definitionFit: To ascend is to go up — a balloon ascends — and the past tense matches went in the definition.

indicatorNotes.cooked: Cooking changes what goes into the pot, so the letters do not come out in the order they went in.
indicatorNotes.around: Around says one piece is written encircling another, the rearranged letters closing over what follows them.

blocks.note: the five letters of ALGAE rearranged
n is the standard short form of noon, as in 12n on a timetable

annotation.surface: Somebody making lunch out of pond weed at midday.
annotation.walkthrough: Girl is the vaguest sort of definition and does no more than announce that a name is coming. Noon for N stands alongside north, name and knight among that letter's regular duties.
annotation.definitionFit: Angela is an ordinary English given name for a woman, which is the whole of what the definition claims.

entries.clue: To make certain, follow around end of October (6)

indicatorNotes.around: Around puts one piece bodily round another, so the word in front is split open to take it in.
indicatorNotes.end of: The end of a word is its final letter, and that single letter is all that is taken from it.

blocks.note: to ensue is to follow, as consequences ensue from an act
the last letter of OCTOBER

annotation.surface: An instruction to tail somebody about as the month runs out.
annotation.walkthrough: Around reads in the surface as at about the end of October, a date rather than an instruction. Ensue and ensure are unrelated words that happen to differ by the one letter October supplies.
annotation.definitionFit: To ensure a thing is to make certain of it, both phrased as infinitives so either can follow I will.
